CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Roberts is a 49-year-old male who presented to the emergency room in March with high blood pressure and palpitations. The patient attributes this episode to consumption of several cups of coffee and fasting on that day, believing it was likely a panic attack rather than a true cardiac event. He reports no recurrence of palpitations since that time. He has a long-standing history of hypertension since he was young. Approximately one month ago, his new primary care physician started him on a combination antihypertensive medication. He checks his blood pressure at home every morning and reports readings consistently in the range of 146-155 mmHg. He is attempting to reduce his salt intake and occasionally exercises on a treadmill.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies recurrent palpitations since March event.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension

MEDICATIONS
Benicar HCT (hydrochlorothiazide 40-25 mg)
Amlodipine 10 mg daily
Spironolactone (newly initiated)

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Strong family history of hypertension in multiple family members

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives with girlfriend. Attempting dietary salt reduction and treadmill exercise when possible.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds good
Pulmonary: Lungs clear
Abdomen: Soft, no tenderness
Extremities: No edema noted in ankles and feet
General: Alert and oriented

RESULTS
Potassium: 4.0 (one week prior)
Thyroid profile from March 1, 2021 (prior results reviewed)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Resistant hypertension on maximal doses of three antihypertensive medications (Benicar HCT, amlodipine, and newly added spironolactone). Patient counseled regarding possible secondary causes of hypertension including hyperaldosteronism. Spironolactone initiated with discussion of potential side effects including dizziness, electrolyte disturbances, and rare gynecomastia (1 in 100 patients). Patient instructed to maintain adequate hydration and to avoid salt intake exceeding 2000 mg daily (goal 1500 mg daily). Recommended DASH diet and heart.org resources. Advised regular treadmill exercise for 30 minutes most days of week, which may reduce blood pressure by 7-10 mmHg. Follow-up appointment scheduled in 2 weeks with repeat blood pressure measurement and metabolic panel to monitor potassium and sodium levels. If inadequate response to spironolactone, next steps include consideration of carvedilol or referral to resistant hypertension clinic for evaluation of secondary causes and possible intervention such as renal denervation.
